clue.text: Hand out punishment?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone dealing out a penalty
setter's reading: a punishment literally dealt to the hand, a mild rebuke

explanation.surface: Someone in authority doling out discipline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hand out' reads as a phrasal verb meaning distribute; really it is a punishment aimed at the hand, a light tap near it.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a token, lenient reprimand, pictured as a light smack delivered to the wrist.

clue.text: Road crew's machines restore small unstable …

indicators.note: unstable letters will not stay put, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Road workers' heavy equipment patching up a small, shaky stretch, running on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small' looks like an abbreviation for S, but the whole word is anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavy rollers flatten new asphalt, so they are machines used by road-building gangs.

clue.text: … crack with tar for free

blocks.note: a tar is a sailor, abbreviated AB for able seaman
to crack a puzzle is to solve it

explanation.surface: Continuing 1 down: road crews fixing a crack with tar.
explanation.walkthrough: Tar is a sailor here, not road surfacing.
explanation.definitionFit: To absolve is to free someone from blame or guilt; 'free' is a verb here.

clue.text: Special unavailable after lunchtime?

blocks.note: one o'clock is a typical lunch hour
a dish that is off the menu is unavailable

explanation.surface: A restaurant's special of the day sold out after the lunch rush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lunchtime' stands for one o'clock, a time read as a number; 'unavailable' is the menu sense of a dish that has run out.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-off is something unique, made or happening only once, hence special.

clue.text: Superior of mine lifted lid …

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifted means read upwards, so the word is turned round

blocks.note: a tip is a spoil heap at a mine
a lid sits on a pot; here lid stands for the topmost part

explanation.surface: The boss at a mine raising a lid, continued into 5 down.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a tip is a heap of waste from a coal mine.
explanation.definitionFit: Tip-top means first-rate or excellent, so it can stand for superior as an adjective.

clue.text: … on elite struggling to capture Conservative vote

indicators.note: struggling letters are in disarray, so they are rearranged
capturing takes something prisoner inside, so the shuffled letters surround the letter

blocks.note: taken as written
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: Continuing 4 down: the elite fighting to win a Tory poll.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'lid' from 4 down is lifted on the elite as it struggles at the ballot.
explanation.definitionFit: An election is a formal poll, the process of voting for candidates.

clue.text: Something to nibble right next to cool bar?

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
to ice something is to cool it
a cake of soap is a bar

explanation.surface: A snack eaten beside a trendy bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cool bar' suggests a fashionable pub; a bar is a cake, as of soap.
explanation.definitionFit: A rice cake is a light puffed-rice snack, the sort of thing one nibbles.

clue.text: Boy reportedly set up clock outside

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard, so a word with the same sound is used
in a down entry, up means read from the bottom, so the letters are turned round

blocks.note: a boy is a son
set as a past tense, put down

explanation.surface: A lad arranging a clock in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside' is part of the definition, not a container indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: A sundial tells the time by a shadow cast by the sun, so it is a garden timepiece.

clue.text: Time running out, tense about United result

indicators.note: something running out is leaving, so the letter for time departs from the word
about means surrounding, so the shortened word goes around the letter for United

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
taken as written
U is the usual abbreviation for United

explanation.surface: A sports report: a tight match, the clock ticking down, then United's final score.
explanation.walkthrough: Take T from TENSE to leave ENSE, then put U inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensue is to follow as a consequence, so 'result' works as a verb here.

clue.text: Cold ear-hole?

blocks.note: first meaning: bitterly sharp, as of a wind
second meaning: a hole made in the ear for jewellery

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read as one complaint about a chilly ear; they are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A biting wind is described as piercing, and a pierced earlobe is called a piercing.

clue.text: Many bound to get into this talk with a bishop in French

definitions.text: Many bound to get into this

blocks.note: rabbit is British slang for chatter
W is the abbreviation for with
taken as written
Right Reverend, a bishop's title
the French word for in

explanation.surface: Many people are sure to talk their way into a French bishop's circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' reads as certain; it is the leaping of rabbits.
explanation.definitionFit: Bounding animals by the dozen enter their underground network of tunnels and burrows.

clue.text: Two drinks in electric vehicle

blocks.note: the first drink, taken from the dairy
the second drink: a soft drink with ice cream floating on it

explanation.surface: Someone sipping a pair of beverages while riding in a car.
explanation.walkthrough: A milk float is the small battery-powered van British milkmen use for doorstep deliveries.
explanation.definitionFit: The milkman's delivery cart has long been battery-driven, a classic electric vehicle on British streets.

clue.text: Ceramic from Zurich in Argos

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of Zurich, all of in, and the start of Argos

explanation.surface: Pottery from a Swiss city spotted in a British catalogue store.
explanation.walkthrough: Argos is a British catalogue shop chain.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine porcelain tableware is called china, a type of ceramic ware.

clue.text: Be in debt to northern poet

blocks.note: to owe is to be in debt
N is the abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: A poet from the north who is short of money.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilfred Owen was a First World War poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilfred Owen wrote celebrated war poetry such as Dulce et Decorum Est.

clue.text: Group examining works wearing protective jackets?

definitions.text: Group examining works wearing protective jackets?

blocks.clueFragment: Group examining works wearing protective jackets?
blocks.note: surface reading: inspectors at a factory in safety gear

blocks.clueFragment: Group examining works wearing protective jackets?
blocks.note: setter's reading: people discussing literary works, which come in dust jackets

explanation.surface: A team of inspectors touring a factory floor in high-visibility vests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Works' suggests a factory and 'jackets' clothing; the works are novels and the jackets are dust covers.
explanation.definitionFit: A reading circle meets to discuss books, which are published wrapped in protective dust jackets.

clue.text: Energy beginning to drain my mains supply

indicators.note: beginning to points to the opening letter of the next word
read as the adverb of supple, meaning flexibly, so the letters bend into a new order

blocks.note: its opening letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Power starting to drain from the household electricity supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like a noun from mains supply; it is suppl(e)y, in a flexible way.
explanation.definitionFit: Dynamism is vigour and drive, a lively force that the word energy also names.

clue.text: Times piece supporting British computer technology, gradually

indicators.note: in a down entry, supporting means placed underneath, so this part follows the next

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for British
information technology
as in three by four, meaning multiplied
a bit is a small piece

explanation.surface: A newspaper article on British tech, written in instalments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper but means multiplied by, as in three by four; in a down entry 'supporting' puts that part below the British computer part.
explanation.definitionFit: Bit by bit means a little at a time, little by little, which is gradual progress.

clue.text: Pick duly random National Lottery option

indicators.note: random means in no set order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to choose properly when playing the lottery.
explanation.walkthrough: In the UK National Lottery, a lucky dip is a ticket whose numbers the machine picks at random.
explanation.definitionFit: Players may choose their own numbers or opt for a computer-chosen selection, which is called this.

clue.text: Amusing card adult left

blocks.note: a card is a joker, a funny person
A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A funny greetings card that a grown-up left behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Card' looks like a greetings card; it is a comic person.
explanation.definitionFit: Comical means funny and laughable, a synonym of amusing as an adjective.

clue.text: Worn-out photograph

blocks.note: first meaning: ruined or exhausted, informally
second meaning: a picture taken with a camera

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a faded old picture, but the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done for is informally 'shot', and a snap taken with a camera is also called this.

clue.text: Summit with no end in sight and mostly sweltering? Oh well!

indicators.note: with no end visible, the final letter of the word is dropped
mostly means not all, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: a summit is a height
sweltering means very hot

explanation.surface: A hiker on an endless climb in the heat, sighing in resignation.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words lose their last T.
explanation.definitionFit: Heigh-ho is a sigh of weary resignation, the same mood as a resigned 'Oh well!'.

clue.text: Watchful when guarding second-class, he was close to Victoria

indicators.note: guarding something means surrounding it, so the first word goes around the letter

blocks.note: watchful means alert
B grade is second class

explanation.surface: A watchful bodyguard for a lesser figure, one who stayed near the queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Prince Albert was Queen Victoria's husband.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Albert was Queen Victoria's consort and closest companion until his death.

clue.text: Say no to landfill?

blocks.note: first meaning: decline
second meaning: rubbish

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an environmental slogan; the two meanings are pronounced differently.
explanation.definitionFit: To refuse is to decline, and refuse as a noun is waste that ends up dumped in the ground.

clue.text: Odd first half to barn dance

indicators.note: first half means only the opening portion of the following word is kept

blocks.note: rum is an old-fashioned word for strange
the first two of its four letters

explanation.surface: A strange start to a country barn dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barn dance' looks like one phrase; 'barn' is wordplay and 'dance' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This lively Cuban ballroom style is a well-known Latin dance.

clue.text: Dancer, 21, cut nail carelessly

indicators.note: cut means trimmed, so the referenced answer loses its final letter
done carelessly, the letters end up jumbled

blocks.note: the answer to 21 down
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dancer who clumsily trims a nail.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the last letter of ALBERT and mix those five letters with NAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballerina is a female ballet performer, so a kind of dancer.

clue.text: I must replace American in game and dash off

indicators.note: must replace says one letter takes another's place in the word

blocks.note: taken as written
A is a common abbreviation for American
the board game of building words from letter tiles

explanation.surface: An instruction to swap a player out of a game and leave in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: In SCRABBLE, the A is swapped for I.
explanation.definitionFit: To scribble is to write hastily, and to dash off a note means the same.

clue.text: Show addict to eat healthily at first

indicators.note: eating takes something inside, so the first word goes around the letter
at first points to the opening letter of the word before it

blocks.note: a user is a drug addict
its opening letter

explanation.surface: Advice to a recovering addict to eat a healthy diet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' is a verb here: to show someone to a seat.
explanation.definitionFit: To usher someone is to guide or show them to where they should go.

clue.text: Sinatra song that Armstrong requested?

blocks.note: surface reading: a jazz trumpeter asking for a Sinatra number
setter's reading: Neil Armstrong, the astronaut, asking to be flown to the lunar surface

explanation.surface: A musician named Armstrong asking for a song made famous by Sinatra.
explanation.walkthrough: Armstrong suggests Louis the trumpeter; it is Neil the astronaut, for whom the song's title would be a travel request.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sinatra standard's title is literally a plea to be carried into space, fitting the first man on the lunar surface.
